## 1. Open the repository in a Codespace

[![Open in GitHub Codespaces](https://github.com/codespaces/badge.svg)](https://codespaces.new/aayancheng/banking-analytics-workshop)

You need a free GitHub account. The first start takes a few minutes: the Codespace
installs every pinned package and then runs the checks once. When the terminal settles,
you are ready.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Prefer your own machine?
Clone the repository, then run `make setup` and `make verify`. You need Python 3.11 or
later. Everything in the course works the same way locally.
:::

## 2. Run the one command

In the Codespace's terminal:

```bash
python verify.py
```

Each line is a check: the Python version, the pinned dependencies, the data, each model's
gate, the documentation and the decision apps. The last line tells you where you are. Every
check that passes has been recomputed from scratch on your machine, just now.

If a check fails, read its last line: it says what failed and prints the command that
repairs it.

## 3. Stage tags: save points you can jump to

The platform was built in stages, and each is a git tag — a permanent bookmark on a moment
in the repository's history. `stage-0` is the empty environment; `stage-5` has everything.
Each tag passes its own `verify.py`, so if your own work goes wrong, or you missed a session,
you can jump to the stage you need and carry on from a working state:

```bash
git stash -u                  # park your own changes (git stash pop brings them back)
git checkout stage-4
git checkout main -- workshop notebooks wiki
python verify.py
```

The third line matters. The workshop sheets, the notebooks and this documentation live on
`main` only — no tag contains them — so a stage jump removes them. Restoring them from
`main` brings them back without moving you off the stage.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Use `git ls-files`, not `ls`, to see what a stage contains
Python leaves cache folders behind that git ignores, so after a jump `ls` can show folders
that are not part of the stage.
:::

To come back to the finished platform: `git checkout main`.

## 4. Choose an agent

The homework in every chapter asks you to direct an AI coding agent, then check what it
produced against the repository. The prompts are written to work with any agent. Two that
the exercises are tested with:

| Agent | Cost | Where |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub Copilot | a free tier is available | built into VS Code, including in a Codespace |
| Claude Code | paid | runs in the Codespace's terminal |

Whichever you use, the rule is the same: an agent's answer is a claim, not a result. The
result is what `python verify.py` says after the agent has finished.
